svg.title: The toolbox checks the test really failed first, instead of taking anyone's word for it: GitLab can read a real failure report even when assertions contain terminal colours
svg.text: The toolbox checks the test really failed first, instead
of taking anyone's word for it
Scenario: GitLab can read a real failure report even when assertions contain terminal colours
GitLab reads the report of a merge request
The RED gate reads the same report

g.text: Given a merge request adds one passing scenario, one plain failure and one failure in
A merge request adds three probe scenarios to a throwaway copy of the toolbox, with the steps behind them. One passes.
Two fail with the same message: quotes, an accent, an emoji, a tab and a line break included.
The last step also wraps its message in terminal colours, the escape code before [31m, and adds every control character
XML forbids: the kind of text a test tool really prints.
When its pipeline runs the three scenarios, and GitLab counts one pass and two failures
The merge request's pipeline runs the three scenarios with the toolbox's own test engine and JUnit reporter, on the very
image the test suite runs in, and hands the report to GitLab.
GitLab reads it without a complaint: 3 tests, 2 failures, 0 errors, and one line per scenario on the junit-probes suite.
Then GitLab shows the coloured failure as readable text, without the terminal colours
The details of the coloured failure, as a reviewer opens them on that tab. The message reads as it was written, with no
escape code and none of the forbidden characters.
And the RED guard still accepts the coloured assertion as a genuine failure
The same three scenarios, run on the developer's machine, leave the same report in project/tests/e2e/_output/junit. The
RED gate reads it and accepts the coloured failure as real: the scenario ran and failed on its own check.
It quotes that check on one readable line: the line break and the tab become spaces, and nothing of the colours is left.
